How we bake sourdough

Flour, water, salt, time, and a starter that has been alive longer than the shop has. The interesting part is the time: everything else can be measured, and time is the ingredient people try to skip.

The starter

Fed twice a day with the same rye it was born on. A starter that has been neglected can be brought back, but it will taste like the neglect for a week.

The bake

Hot, steam for the first ten minutes, then dry. A loaf that goes in without steam looks fine and cuts badly, which is the closest thing baking has to a silent failure.

Why the interval matters more than the amount

A starter fed on a schedule rises predictably, and predictability is the whole reason to keep one rather than opening a packet of yeast. Feeding twice as much half as often does not average out: the culture spends the long gap consuming what is left and turning acidic, and an acidic starter raises bread more slowly and tastes sharper than most people intend.

What the smell tells you

Acetone means hungry. The smell is ethanol and acetic acid accumulating because the available starch has been eaten, and the fix is two feeds twelve hours apart rather than throwing the jar away. Sweet and yeasty means recently fed and near its peak, which is when it should go into a dough. Nail polish and a grey liquid on top means it has been ignored for weeks, and even that is usually recoverable.

Storing between bakes

Refrigerate it with a loose lid. Cold slows fermentation without stopping it, so a weekly feed is enough to keep a culture alive for years. Feed it twice at room temperature before you plan to bake, and give the second feed at least four hours so it is rising rather than falling when it meets the flour.
